sets.title: Working from home
text: Working from home has become much more common {{1}} the last few years. Many employees now spend {{2}} two or three days a week at home instead of travelling to an office.
One of the main advantages is {{3}} people can organise their own time more freely. {{4}} they are careful, however, they can end up working longer hours than before.

{{5}} most workers say they enjoy the extra freedom, a few admit {{6}} they sometimes feel lonely without colleagues nearby. Companies {{7}} offer home working usually ask staff to attend the office at least once a week.
It is still too early to say {{8}} this way of working will continue once the current trend fades.

questions.explanation: 'Over/in/during the last few years' are all common ways to describe a recent period of time.
'Around'/'about' both mean 'approximately'; 'between' also works before 'two and three days'.

commonWrong.almost: 'Almost two or three days' is not a natural combination with 'or'.

questions.explanation: 'That' introduces the clause explaining what the advantage actually is.

commonWrong.what: 'What' cannot be used here because the sentence already has its own subject, 'people'.

questions.explanation: 'If' introduces the condition under which people might end up working longer hours.
'While/although/whereas' all introduce a contrast with the idea in the second half of the sentence.
'Admit that' is the usual pattern for reporting what someone confesses.
'That/which' is the relative pronoun referring back to 'companies'.
'Whether' introduces the indirect question about whether the trend will continue.

commonWrong.if: 'If' is possible in informal speech but 'whether' is the standard form after 'say' in writing.
